title: Bram and the Big Log
markdown:
The Whispering Willows used to be Bram the beaver’s favourite spot. His burrow sat tight under the roots of an old twisty oak, only a hop, skip, and splash across the bubbling brook. Today the brook had delivered a grumpy giant. A log so thick it would take three Brams to hug it, heavy as a hundred autumn leaves, lay right across the entrance to his cozy home. All his winter stores—the sweetest bark, the tastiest roots—waited on the other side, locked away by this unwelcome visitor.

“Oh, whiskers,” Bram said. His tidy fur drooped like wet moss. He nudged the log with his broad flat tail. Not an inch. He tried gnawing one end, but his sharp teeth bounced off the tough bark. “It’s no use.” A nervous tremor ran through his chest. The cold wind had begun to whisper winter, and without his food he would not be ready.

Lark the kingfisher, a flash of blue on a willow branch, saw the struggle. Iridescent feathers caught the light as he swooped down and landed with a soft flutter. “What’s the trouble, Bram?” His voice was clear as a small bell.

Bram pointed a damp paw. “This log. I can’t move it, and all my winter food is trapped inside.” He pushed again. Strong beaver legs scrabbled the muddy bank. The log stayed. Lark, always curious, fluttered up and circled slowly, studying every angle.

“Wait a minute, Bram. Look over there.” He pointed his beak at a mossy grey rock. Leaning against it, as if forgotten, was a long straight branch, longer than Bram was tall, and wonderfully sturdy. Near it lay a round smooth stone the size of a juicy apple. “That branch looks strong. And that stone…”

Bram’s whiskers twitched. He shuffled to the branch, paws sinking in soft earth. It was indeed strong. He looked at the stone, perfectly smooth, sun-warmed. He nudged it, and it rolled easily on its curve. He remembered kin using smaller logs to tilt bigger ones, and rocks to prop dam-work. This felt different. This felt interesting.

“What if we use that long branch, and that round stone?”

He rolled the stone close to the giant log and set it just so. Then, with all his might, he nudged one end of the branch under the massive wood until the branch rested on the stone. The stone, he saw, was a tiny helpful mountain for the stick.

“All right, Lark. Watch this.” He moved to the far end, the end that stuck out away from the log, gathered himself, took a firm stance, and pushed down.

The massive log wobbled. It lifted. Bram pushed harder. The branch held. The log tilted. Then came a rumble—scraping wood and mud, bark biting earth—as the giant began to move. With a final heave Bram pushed the branch as far as it would go. The log rolled, and the burrow’s mouth stood clear.

“We did it.” Bram splashed in the cool water, relief washing through him. “The branch and stone made it so much easier.”

Lark landed beside him, bobbing. “That was amazing. How did you know that would work?”

Bram’s tail gave a happy flick. “It’s called a lever. The long branch was a strong arm. The stone was a helper’s shoulder, right where it needed to be. When I pushed down on one end, the other end lifted the heavy log. Like a seesaw for really big jobs. That is why a crowbar shifts a crate, and why a playground seesaw lifts a friend.”

He looked at the cleared entrance, then at Lark, eyes bright with new understanding. The winter stores waited, safe. The log, now a neighbour instead of a door, lay where a lever had told it to go. Bram wondered what else a long arm and a well-placed stone might teach a beaver who had thought, for one frightened morning, that the only tools he owned were teeth.
